drills.q: Where does a file's name live?
options: In a directory, which is a file holding names paired with inode numbers
In the inode
In the superblock's name table
In the first block of the file
drills.why: The inode has no name, which is why two names can refer to one file and neither is the original.

drills.q: What does removing a name do?
options: Decrements a count; the inode is freed when nothing refers to it
Frees the inode and its blocks
Marks the inode for deletion at the next unmount
Zeroes the file's blocks
drills.why: And the count is not the only reference: a descriptor holds the file too, which is why a deleted log can keep a disk full while a process is still writing to it.

drills.q: Appending to a file is four separate writes. What is the danger of a crash between them?
options: A structure that is self-contradictory, such as a block in a file and also in the free list
Losing the appended data
A file with the wrong size
A directory entry with no inode
drills.why: Leaked space is recoverable by a scan. A block in two files is not, and by the time anybody notices, both have been written.

options: Records the whole change, flushes it, then applies it, then marks it done
Records every write for later auditing
Buffers writes until they can be done contiguously
Keeps a copy of the previous version of each block
drills.why: There is no window where a partial change survives without the instructions to finish it, and the cost is that everything is written twice.

drills.q: What does a journalled filesystem cover by default?
options: Metadata only: the inode, the free map, the directory entries
Metadata and data
Data only
Whatever was written since the last flush
drills.why: Your file's contents are not in the journal at all. They are written to their final location and ordered relative to the metadata, and that ordering is the only guarantee.

drills.q: After a crash mid-write on a metadata-journalled filesystem, what do you have?
options: A consistent filesystem and a file containing a mixture of old and new bytes
A consistent filesystem and an intact file
An inconsistent filesystem that needs checking
A truncated file
drills.why: Every check the filesystem performs afterwards passes, because there are no problems of the kind it looks for.

drills.q: What does the default write ordering actually buy?
options: Data blocks reach the medium before the metadata referencing them
That your update is complete or absent
That writes complete in the order issued
Nothing; the ordering is an implementation detail
drills.why: It prevents an inode pointing at blocks still holding a previous file's contents, which would be a security problem as much as a correctness one.

drills.q: What is the only mutation in a copy-on-write update?
options: The root pointer
The block being changed
The inode
The free map
drills.why: Until it switches nothing has changed, and after it everything has, so there is no partial state to recover from and no journal to write.

drills.q: What does copy on write get almost free?
options: Snapshots and data checksums
Contiguous allocation
Smaller metadata
Faster small writes
drills.why: Keeping the old root keeps the whole old tree, and a block never modified in place keeps its checksum valid. It costs fragmentation and the space held by old roots.

drills.q: How does an extent differ from a block list?
options: It records a start and a length, so its size follows the number of runs
It records the file's total size only
It is a compressed block list
It stores blocks indirectly through a tree
drills.why: A contiguous gigabyte is one extent and 262144 list entries. Fully fragmented, extents are worse than the list they replaced.

drills.q: A device returns different bytes than were written and reports no error. Who notices?
options: Only a filesystem that checksums data
The device driver
The page cache, on the next read
Nobody, ever
drills.why: A cable, a controller bug, or a write that landed at the wrong offset all produce data that reads back fine and is wrong, and a backup of it is a corrupted backup.

options: Seeing the whole file before choosing blocks, so they can be contiguous
Reducing the number of system calls
Avoiding the journal for small files
Deferring the durability decision to the application
drills.why: It also widens the window between a write returning and anything being decided about where the data goes.

drills.q: Why did delayed allocation break applications that were working?
options: They renamed without flushing, and the old behaviour happened to write the data first
It introduced a bug in the allocator
It changed the meaning of fsync
It reordered directory updates
drills.why: A crash could leave a correctly named, empty file where a complete one used to be. The guidance was always that a rename without a flush guarantees nothing.

drills.q: What was the resolution to that argument?
options: The filesystem special-cased the pattern, and the guidance to applications did not change
Delayed allocation was removed
Applications were required to use a new call
fsync was made implicit on rename
drills.why: Both positions were defensible, and the practical outcome was that the common pattern got a special case while remaining unguaranteed.

drills.q: What does a filesystem protect, and what is yours?
options: It protects its own structure; your file's contents are your responsibility
It protects both, once the journal is enabled
It protects your data and leaves metadata to the device
Neither, without a copy-on-write filesystem
drills.why: That distinction is the whole unit, and it decides what you have to do yourself: flush the file, and flush the directory.
